`chain xs identity λl → List.push l 3` stay accepted, where the value may hold duplicates the write cannot reach.

Before this, no check saw a duplicate the callee made or passed: `sep` was `yes` by default, and the code's own `K.req` read
a supply through `expand`, which gives a value's objects each once (`no_routes`, §2.11.2). So `[ a, a ]` was one object
behind `app`, `Maybe.map` or any callee that calls a callback once, and `app [ a, a ] λl → List.update l 0 push1` pushed `a`
twice in place on master too. Counting positions at the caller cannot close it: `[ v, v ]` built in the callee is one
arrival at `[*]`, and the contract records no multiplicity. Sound because every value a label is handed is, at the call
that hands it, a value of that frame; the check there sees every position; and a selection it leaves is instantiated at
each frame outward, so a caller's own `[ a, a ]` fails there, at its own positions. Inside a `taken` row's label
(`upd rs f = List.update rs 1 λ( a, b ) → f ( a, b )`) one element is supplied, so the claim holds of that element and not
of the row's family: passed on there, `below` is asked apart, and each write still asks its own slot plain through
`takenOccs` (§2.13.6). Otherwise rows that share a key the callback does not write would be refused. Fixtures
`run/SanitiserOnceCallbackShared` (without `below`, the sanitised run traps) and `run/SanitiserOnceCallbackApart`.

**The answer held by the builder.** A label's condition is instantiated at the recursive call that passes the label on
(§2.11.3), and there `π6` is `put b i (f x)`: the builder holds the answer of the frame's own call, which §2.9.3 reads
as any object at all, so the condition was `no`. An answer of the frame's label whose call's one object argument is an
element taken out of an argument whose elements the condition selects plain and deep (`Fed.covering`) is dropped from
the instantiation, through one level of a call that holds it, and the frame's function joins the condition, deep and
apart. Sound because unknown code answers from what it was handed and what its closure holds. What it was handed is
that element, a part of the plain occurrence, which already asks each of its objects to occur once among all the
selected occurrences. What its closure holds is apart from them by the occurrence added. Nothing else reaches a code:
a write of a top-level value is refused, and `⊤` holds only what has escaped, and an escaped object is refused.

**A cell's contents are a list the condition can read, since the contents relation (#1991, §2.13.7).** A condition over what a cell holds reads what `Ref.make` was given, or an answer as the cell's own. That is sound because a store that may hold one object twice makes the contents escape: after `Ref.set c [ a, a ]`, `Ref.update c λr → List.map r push1` is refused `escaped`, at the caller too when a helper makes the edit (`run/SanitiserTakenElementCell`). `CellEdit.elementEdit`, which refused every write through a `◆` then a `[*]` while v2 could not tell, is gone, so an element of a list in a cell is edited in place when its stores keep the elements apart.

*Amended 2026-11-05 (#2013, #2025): **An answer handed on.*** A label's answer in another label's supply (`y = f x; g y`)
was never judged: `unknown` as a whole, the kept check skipped it, and nothing asked that two runs of a label get two objects. So
`chain x f g = ( y = f x; ( g y, g y ) )` with `λw → w` and a writer pushed one list twice in place, and so did `( g y, y )`,
`( g (f x), x )`, `[ y ]` and a closure over `y` held beside `g y`. Unknown code answers what it was handed or what its closure
holds, or makes something, so there are three rules, and the third asks of the code the caller knows.

1. **A holder of the answer keeps the supply.** The answer is judged as a supplied part with the relation read the other way
   (`AnswerKeep.kept`): the same call's answer, in a local, an operand or a pending operand, is `may`; another label's answer that
   was handed it is `may` under that function's `fresh`; anything else is what §2.9.2 step 7 says the answer may hold, and where
   that is not `no`, `fresh` of the function that answered. The answer may also be whatever its call was supplied and whatever its
   function holds, so those are judged too, each as a supplied part (`Supplied.mayBeHeld`): one held after the call, or apart from a
   holder only under a selection, asks the same `fresh`. A selection of the holder is not asked instead: at a recursive call it reads
   the accumulator that already holds earlier answers, and no such selection can hold. The same holds of an answer in a callee: a pass
   whose callee supply arrives from another label's answer judges that answer against what the frame holds after the call, with no
   operands, since the call's arguments are the callee's to judge (`( pipe x f g, x )`, `pipe x f g = g (f x)`). A label's own answer
   at a pass is §2.11.3's feedback.
2. **`fresh`** is the `fed` occurrence with no argument, printed `π2{ε!}`: the function at `π2ε` answers only objects it makes.
   §2.11.3's rule for `fed` decides it at a known code, with no argument to allow, and it passes on as `fed` does. A fresh object is
   apart from every object that existed before it, and each run makes its own. A `top-level`, a capture and an argument all fail it.
3. **A function that runs more than once may answer one object each time.** Where a supply holds the answer of a label whose function
   runs at least twice in the frame (direct calls, passes and outer labels add up as `calls` does), the supply's `sep` asks that the
   answers be apart (`SupplyAnswers.repeated`): `ε!k` with that label's own `sep` and `below`, when it has one supply and keeps none of
   it, since then each answer is a part of what that run was handed; `fresh` otherwise. A label's own answer handed back to it is
   §2.11.3's feedback and asks `fed` as before. So `( g (f x), g (f x) )` with `λ_ → k`, and `List.map xs λ_ → g (f x)`, are refused,
   and `twice f x = f (f x)` with a writer stays accepted.

**A capture handed to a label in a code run many times.** `chain xs y g = List.map xs λ_ → g y` hands `y` to `g` once per element. The
closure holds `y` for its next run, exactly as it does when the code writes the capture, which is `once`. So a capture supplied to a
label passed on inside a code run more than once keeps the slot, at the pass (`Supplied.heldByClosure`). A code runs more than once when
an outer label is many, when two labels of that call have one function slot (`two h = ( h ⊤, h ⊤ )`, which `LabelChain.outwardMany` now
adds up). What the callee holds across the run is judged too: a capture supplied, or an answer in a known code, has as operands what
§2.11.3 *a capture written across the callee's run* gives a capture write (`Across.operands`), so `pair (λ⊤ → g y) y` and `both (λ⊤ → g1 y)
(λ⊤ → g2 y)` keep the slot. No argument is left out for an answer: a callee keeps one (`pair2 l p = ( p l, l )`), hands one element and holds the rest (`sel xs p = case xs
of [ h, …t ] → ( p h, t )`), or, as `List.update`, returns the other positions, and a contract tells none of these from a traversal. So
`List.map xs λv → g (f v)` and `List.update xs i λv → g (f v)` are refused with `f` an identity, sound or not (#2046).

Refused that a perfect checker accepts: an answer of a capture beside a held argument the capture is not (`( g (f x), x )` with `λ_ → k`);
two answers of an identity over apart arguments, `( g (f x), g (f y) )` with `λw → w`, since only `fresh` is asked of a holder;
one fresh answer per run over a list with a duplicate, because `ε!k` also asks the supply's `below`; and a chain of two different
functions over one label (`g (f (g x))`). Sound because the three sources are all an answer can be (§2.9.2 step 7): a holder of the
answer itself is `may`; what its call was handed and what its function holds are judged or asked `fresh`; another run's answer is asked by
rule 3. Fixtures `run/SanitiserAnswerHandedOn` (every case traps or differs under the sanitiser on master) and its twin
`run/SanitiserAnswerHandedOnApart`, where the function makes its own object, runs once, or answers an apart element.

*Amended 2026-11-05 (#2017): **A pass closes what it describes.*** At a pass at the call's function type, read-off describes a callee
supply's `.param` arrivals by structure and drops the entry's open mark (`ReadOff`, `at_site`). An arrival of another kind stays at the
entry's slot, so a write below that slot lands on none of it. That is not a hole, by this invariant, which `SupplyAnswers.closesAtSite`
checks under runtime safety on every closed entry:

- an entry is open only at a type variable's place or a family (§2.10 *Read-off*). Anywhere else `describe` wrote its structure out, and
  there is nothing to close;
- a callee's value at such a slot that is no `.param` is `fresh`, or a label's answer, `⊤`, a loan, a host object or a top-level value.
  `fresh` is the callee's own object, which no caller holds. Every other one gives the distinct check `no` (§2.9.3: a family's answer,
  `shared`; an entry holding `⊤` stays open at the pass, since `⊤` is unknown below its slot), so at the direct call the supply publishes `below no`, unless the arrival is the label's own answer under `fed`, which
  holds only what `.param` arrivals describe, or fresh objects;
- `below` instantiated at a pass stays `no`, and a write below a supply's root asks it (`Outward.finishDemands`).

So a write the close loses is refused `disjoint`, or `unknown` when it has no target at all, even over fresh data, which is where the
precision goes. Fixture: `run/SanitiserAnswerHandedOn`'s last line. The check held over the ledger's 2 300 roots and the oracle.

**As built: an `entry` function's list stays held, until S7 (#1020).** v2 makes no demand at an `entry` argument, so no
caller judges a write of a parameter of `update`, `view` or `init`, and the kept supply was all that stopped a traversal
editing the model: `init = λ⊤ → [ a, a ]` with `update msg m = List.map m λl → List.push l 1` trapped on the first click,
and a `view` that maps over the model trapped with no sharing at all. So a contract records `taken_write`: a many label's
element write, at this level or in a callee, that reaches a parameter. A function value so marked, handed to a parameter
worded `entry`, or held by a closure handed there (its captures may run it), is refused `call` at that call
(`EntryHeld.zig`), where v1 refuses the same programs; a frame that hands its own parameter on is marked `entry` in turn. A list `update` makes for itself is not reached from an argument, and is
edited in place (`browser/tea/EntryFreshTraversal`). A function in a top-level record or a call's answer is refused
`unknown` already (§2.11.3). This holds the line and fixes nothing else: `List.push m 1` in `view` misbehaves on master and
here (#2004). S7's demands replace this rule. Fixture: `ownership/EntryTakenElement`.

Sound in full because every object a taken write reaches is judged. Against the callee, by the holders that keep it
and by Lemma 1's split clause for the container (O9's pinned obligation on every body that reads a `taken` result: the
seven loops of `core/List`). Between invocations, by `π1[*]*`: a write of one element reaches nothing another
element holds, which the next invocation would read. Against the code's own holds, by `K.req` instantiated over the
whole family, and by `below` for what the callee made. Against the caller, by the `callsite` demand. Through a helper, by §2.11.3's passes: the condition is
instantiated at the pass, and the helper's own read of the list keeps the slot.

Measured (2026-11-05, Debug, against master at `89acc9741`). Accepted: C.6's first row over a parameter and a local,
its `edit` row, and the same shapes through `indexedMap`, `filterMap`, `concatMap`, `foldl`, `foldr`, a helper, nested
maps, a field and a tuple's part, all in place (`run/SanitiserTakenElementApart`, refused on master). Refused:
`run/SanitiserTakenElement`, whose probed shapes trap when the supply's condition is not asked. The oracle's 2 638
probes: 0 DIFF, and 3 TRAP, of #1986 and #2013, which trap on master too and hold no traversal. Three generated sweeps,
9 602 programs: 0 TRAP, 0 DIFF, none master accepts refused, 1 465 master refuses accepted. The ledger of 2 298 roots:
11 positions refused → accepted, 2 accepted → refused, each a call into a callee whose own write both sides refuse:
`Differential`'s `t42Repeated`, whose `[ tags, tags ]` master accepted only because it refused the write inside `t42`, and
`BallMachine`'s `Ref.modify` of `step`, refused at `Physics` 299:14. Cost: growth unchanged everywhere, `Schema.shapeOf`
+157 records of 229 045.
Refused that a perfect checker accepts: rows that share a part the callback does not write, because the condition is
deep and plain and not per written slot, as `takenOccs` is for `List.update`; and an edit of the elements of a list
`List.map` answered or `List.reverse` built, because a result's separation is another rule (Appendix C.6, *As built*).

*Amended 2026-11-05 (#1979, #2046): **a traversal's supply.*** Nothing in a contract told a traversal from any other label: `map`'s
supply and `app v f = f v`'s read alike, and so did `List.map` and `sel xs p = case xs of [ h, …t ] → ( p h, t )`. A supply now says
so: printed `[1 each: …]`, the `each` mark on `Contract.Supply`, or `[1 walk: …]` where the stronger `walk` holds too, block version 24.
Both are derived from the walk, never from a name.

**What `each` says.** In one activation of the callee, every run of the label is handed at `k` one element of one family
`π_j·p[*]` of a parameter (E1), no position of that family is handed twice (E2), and no holder of the callee reaches the element
after the run (E3). The claim is about positions: `[ a, a ]` has two positions, and whether the two hold one object is the
family's own condition, which the caller asks. E3 is the supply having no `kept` slot. **`walk`** adds E4: the callee reads the family
only to hand it over. A contract's `reads` cannot say that (`shows t` and a walk both read `π1ε*`), and no position's holder is a holder of
another position, so E3 does not imply it. So `walk` comes only from a `taken` row, which the index obligation pins (§2.13.6).

**How it is derived** (`Traversal.zig`, at the read-off, after the labels' kept slots). Supply `k` of a label of the frame is `each` when
`kept` is empty, nothing but one parameter's arrivals at or below a `[*]` arrive at it, and its sources are these:

- a **direct call** whose argument `k` is the result of a `taken` row, or a pattern's `front` position of a value. At most one direct call.
- a **pass** to a callee's supply that is `each`, over a value of the frame: the source is that value (its own slot, or a `slice`
  position of it), read through a call only where that call answers its parameter whole, unwritten (`base`, `Each.answersWhole`): any
  other call's result is no walk of what it was handed (`List.map (dbl xs) f`). Two passes must walk one value: then they are alternatives, since a holder of that value at the first, the
  second pass's argument, would have kept the first's supply. Inside a known code, the code must be run once by every label
  outward, or its argument must be that label's `each` supply, level by level (`Traversal.runsEach`): `List.map rss λrs → List.map rs f`
  is one traversal of `rss[*][*]`, and `List.map ys λ_ → List.map xs f` hands `xs` once per `ys`, and is none.
- a known code that **hands on** its own argument: a pass whose callee label is `once`, keeps nothing, and has the code's own
  parameter whole at its root, where the label running the code is `each` at that parameter (`mp rs f = List.map rs λv → f v`).

`walk` holds when every source is a `taken` element, or a pass of a `walk` supply over a value whole, outside a known code: a holder of that
value after the pass keeps its supply, and a pattern's `front` is held by nothing that would, so `[ x, …rest ]` never gives it.

A direct call and a pass together must name different positions: a `taken` element and a pass over its container whole are
one traversal by the index obligation (§2.13.6, pinned); a pattern's `front` at `i` and a `slice` from `j > i` of the same value are
apart by their positions (§2.3.2). Anything else is no traversal: `go xs f = case xs of [ x, …_ ] → [ f x, …go xs f ]` hands `x` again.
In a group the mark starts from the first round's own sources and only falls, as a condition does (`within` refuses a claim
of `each` a walk does not give; a join is the conjunction). So `mapHelp`, its sisters, and a hand-written `myMap` over `[ x, …rest ]` are `each`; `filter`, `partition` and `map2`
are not, their labels' supplies being `kept`, and `any` is not, as it reads with `at`, which makes no split.

**What it licenses, so far.**

1. **A row's unwritten parts stay in the row (#1979).** A `callsite` write through an `each` supply asks of the family only what a `taken`
   row's does (§2.13.6, `RowEnv.takenOccs`): the family's occurrences of `sep` and `below` are read apart (`Each.relaxed`), and the
   written slot plain. A write that names no slot of the supply, deep at the root of a supply described by structure (`Ref.make v`
   of a row whose entries are `.0`, `.1`), relaxes nothing and asks `sep` and `below` as they stand. All of it is **one selection**: instantiated one by one, the plain slot is never compared with what the
   function holds, `π2{ε*~}`, and `List.map [ a, [ 2 ] ] λl → List.push l (List.length a)` reads the edited `a` (it did, in the first
   build). So `List.map [ ( k, [ 1 ] ), ( k, [ 2 ] ) ] λ( a, b ) → ( a, List.push b 3 )` is accepted in place, and the same call writing `a` is
   refused. Only a call that applies the code relaxes: at a pass the plain condition is instantiated on the argument and stored
   as it is, so a callee's own `[ ( k, j ), ( k, j ) ]` handed to a parameter's function is `no` there, and its supply is not `each` anyway
   (`fresh` and the parameter's slots arrive at it, E1).
2. **What the callee holds of the family (#2046).** An answer in a known code run by a label is judged against what the callee may hold
   across the run (§2.11.3, *A capture handed to a label*). Now an argument `j` that a label **takes** is left out of those operands:
   a `walk` supply hands its whole family, and it reaches no result, store or escape of the callee (`Each.takes`). `List.map xs λv → g (f v)` with `f` an identity is
   accepted. `sel` is not left out: its supply is no `walk`, as neither is a hand-written walker's, and a callee that hands `h` and
   then reads `t` (`y = p h`, `shows t`) would read what the answer wrote. A capture keeps every argument as an operand: a capture
   is no element, and rule 3 of *An answer handed on* still asks what a repeated function answers.

3. **The answers of distinct runs over apart elements are apart (#1978, #2007, #2031).** A result that holds a label's answers was `no`:
   an answer is unknown code's, and a family of them is any object at all. A contract now keeps a second condition, `res_read`,
   printed `answers ⇐ …`, only where `res_cond` is `no`: the result's separation with its answers **read**. Reading is a second run of
   the distinct check (§2.9.3, `Answers.zig`), asked only where the first says `no` and met an answer, a `taken` element or a call with a `res_read`
   on the way (`Relation.read_mode`). A call's kept condition and a pair's value are per mode, since an ask outside a check may fall back to
   reading (`Distinct.modeOf`). The first run, and every call inside it, is exactly the old one: a call that vouches
   is read differently from one that does not, so a selection in place of `no` inside a check would refuse what the old check took apart.
   Only the outcome `no` of a whole check can change, and only to a condition that also holds. A recursive code with no label and no `taken`
   row publishes no `res_read`: it has no answer of its own, and `Schema.shapeOf` paid for its calls' reading over nine rounds, past its
   limit. Such a result stays `no`, a precision gap, never a change of what is checked.

   An answer is read as what its run was handed, deep, and the check gathers the **answers occurrence** `π_j{s!!k}` (`s!!` with no object
   argument, `Contract.occAns`). A direct call's answer needs at most one object argument. A passed-on label's needs at most one object supply, `each`
   or `once`: otherwise (`rep n x f = [ f x, …rep (n - 1) x f ]`) it stays an answer and meets everything. A `taken` element's and an `each`
   supply's parts are read **apart**, entries of one family that are never compared; anything else is read plain, so `[ f x, f x ]` meets
   itself. An answer met twice (`y = f ⊤; [ y, y ]`) is `no`, and so are the apart reads of two functions, whose occurrences would
   each ask their family in a selection of their own. A `taken` element's expansion is not compared with its container's family in this
   reading (the index obligation), so `reverse` and `filter` read `π1{[*]*}`.

   The occurrence is decided at a caller (`Answers.at`), over every label of the function slot in **one** selection: at a label that
   passes on it renames; at a known code `K` it asks `K`'s own result separation (`λ_ → ( a = [ 1 ]; [ a, a ] )` fails it) and reads `K`'s
   result. `fresh` asks nothing. `K`'s argument `k` asks that supply's arrivals plain and deep, in the selection of the callee's other occurrences, and is `no` where the
   supply's own `sep` or `below` is: `List.map (dupL a) f` repeats its family inside the callee, where nothing that renames the occurrence would ask it.
   A capture that holds an object at the slot, read from the capture's own position, is `no`. A label `K` passes on renames, and one `K` applies is read the same way. Anything else is `no`. So
   `List.map xs λ_ → [ 1 ]` holds whatever `xs` is (C.6), `List.map xs λl → l` asks `xs`'s elements apart, and `λ_ → k` is `no`.
   A supply's `below` is never read: a pass that closes an entry relies on it staying `no` (*A pass closes what it describes*), and `comp f g x = g (f x)`
   would otherwise hand a write below `[ s, s ]` to nothing that asks it (a generated sweep's 60 traps).
   A result of nothing but fresh answers asks only that occurrence, so the check stops expanding that call (`Answers.allMade`): expanded, a tuple of
   `n` answers costs `n`, and `wk f = ( w(k-1) f, w(k-1) f )` doubled with the depth. Its entries stay in their group, so one object read twice
   out of the result still meets itself (`[ fst d, fst d ]`).

 Take a known code `K` applied at the caller to a label with an `each` supply, over positions `P` of the
family. By induction on the walk's sources, each run gets a distinct position: one direct call's position and a pass's positions are disjoint
by the case that allowed them, the pass's own by the callee's `each`, alternatives never both run, and a code run once a
level hands on its one element. Then for license 3, by the case split. A run's answer holds only what it was handed and what it made, by the occurrence decided from `K`'s result.
Made objects are new per run. What it was handed is one element, at a position no other run has, so two runs' parts are apart exactly under the family's
plain condition, which the decision asks when and only when `K` answers it; a non-traversal answer's parts are compared as entries. Inside one run, `K`'s own
separation keeps each object once. Against every other entry: an entry apart from what was handed is apart from the answer, and a made object from
every object that existed before it. A capture answered is the one way the same object comes back, and it is refused. For license 1: a write by run `r` reaches, in the family, only objects at its written slot
of its own element, each of which occurs once among the family and every apart occurrence, by the plain occurrence. So no other
run's element, whatever else it shares, reaches the written object, and what the function holds is asked apart in that one selection.
For license 2: `f`'s answer is one object of what `f` was handed or held. The callee's holders of the family after the run reach only other
elements, and read each only to hand it over (E4), once (E2); that element's run is judged at its own call, and a repeated
`f` answers apart by rule 3. `takes` excludes every other way for the callee to reach the family after it returns.

Fixtures: `run/SanitiserTraversal` (the written key, an element handed twice, a callee that returns the rest, one that reads it after
the run, a deep write through a structural supply, two maps of one list: each refused, and each traps without its rule) and
`run/SanitiserTraversalApart` (rows sharing a key, directly, through a helper and a walker; `List.map xs λv → g (f v)`: accepted in place).

*Amended 2026-11-05 (#2032): **a fold's storage.*** A fold's accumulator is the one supply that is the same object from run to run, by the `fed`
occurrence of *a label's answer handed back to it*. That occurrence asked the whole answer to be the argument `k` or fresh, and the
condition asked the accumulator's every object once and apart from the elements. So `List.foldl xs [] λx a → List.push a x`, whose answer holds `x`
at `[*]`, was refused, and `List.foldl xs (List.foldr xs [] …) …` too, whose accumulator holds what the elements are. The write reaches none of that: it
writes `a`'s storage. So a write of a supply with its own `fed` occurrence (`FedWrite.zig`) is asked by the slot it writes. The occurrence is
decided at the written slots: an answer's entry matters where a later run writes it, at a prefix of the written words, or below them for a deep write
(`FedCall.Written`). The supply's own arrivals are read apart, and the written object plain, in one selection, without the deep mark a type variable's
slot gives: below the code's own type it is one object. Everything else in the condition stands, and the function's holds stay in it. A `fed` that renames
at a pass keeps its whole form: a hand-off through another label asks the whole answer.

Sound. A run's write of `a` at slots `W` reaches the objects at `W` of what it was handed: the first value, or an earlier run's answer. The occurrence at `W`
says an answer holds at `W` only the argument's objects, at any slot of it, or fresh ones: a `Dict`'s rotation moves nodes between slots, so the slot is not
compared. A move across slots is judged in the code that makes it, whose write's target reaches, through the group's fixpoint, what its other operands reach
(`( b, List.push a x )` is refused there, and so is an object made twice). So by induction every run writes the first value's object at `W`, or an
object one run made, once. The plain occurrence keeps the first value's apart from everything else in the selection, the elements and what the
function holds. An element stored at `[*]` is only ever read: a code that writes `[*]` has `[*]` in `W`, its answer's `[*]` holds its other argument there, and the
occurrence is `no`. So the fold element's condition stays `lost` (C.9 gap 3), and an element write of the result is refused, as `run/FoldOverFoldShared`
and `run/FeedbackPrevTwice` require. Fixtures: `run/SanitiserFoldStored` (the first value read after, elements written, an element answered and pushed
onto, a capture answered: refused) and `run/SanitiserFoldStoredApart`, `ownership/FoldStoresElements`.

*Amended 2026-11-05 (#2028, #2029, #2030): **a function value in a result.*** A closure a declaration returns was
followed by nobody: `res ε fresh π1ε` says what it holds and nothing of what it does, so at `g = mk xs` the call `g ⊤`
was unknown code. Its answer was `⊤`, and whatever its code answered was refused `unknown` or `alias` at every write
(`GrowFresh`, `CallFeedbackGeneration`, a `List.copy` of the answer). Function slots of a result now have a contract.

**The called contract.** For a declaration's code `D` and a function slot `s` of its result (*Which slots*, below), the
**called contract** `D@s` is what one call of the value at `s` does, as a code of its own, a **called code**. Its
parameters are, in order, the function type's own parameters (`own`, as a closure's own come first), `D`'s parameters
and captures, and one more, **`self`**: the function value itself, a closure-kinded parameter that is read deep. So
`D@s` is a closure code whose captures are everything that made the value, and a value of it is an ordinary closure
value: `built(closure, D@s, kids = (D's arguments at that call, the value))`. It carries what the task of the call
needs to know: its answer, its reads, escapes and stores, its labels and its conditions. A call of it is a code call
(§2.11.2), with its count and its supplies, and a label applied to it a virtual call (§2.11.3), by the rules that
already stand. `grow` above gives `grow@ε`: `res ε fresh`; `mk xs = λ⊤ → xs` gives `mk@ε`: `res ε π2ε`.

**How it is read off.** `D@s` is read off a second walk of `D`'s body, which ends in a call: the value at `s` of the
result, applied to `own`. That call is the walk's **last call**. It is walked as `g own` would be (a closure: a code
call; a choice: each arm; a parameter: a label; anything else: unknown code, whose arguments escape). Everything the
walk made before it is the **creation**. The read-off keeps only what the last call does, its virtual calls included:

- The creation's demands, escapes, reads, labels and closures are `D`'s, instantiated at `D`'s call, and are not said
  again. `D@s` makes no verdict line: a code that writes its own parameter or a capture is refused where the closure
  leaves `D` (§2.11.4), whatever `D@s` says.
- An object the creation made (a site, a creation call's `fresh`), or the answer of a label the creation called, was
  made once, when the value was, so it is not fresh at each call: it arrives as `π_self ε`, deep, *what the value holds*.
  The value holds it by §2.11.4 (`built(closure)` kids; `res` says every object of a capture at the closure's slot), so
  at the caller it is that object, or more. An escape of one is an escape of `self`. A write of one is said by nothing:
  a capture write is refused where the closure leaves `D`, and a cell operation stales no reader (§2.11.4).
- A `fresh` arrival of the last call or of a virtual call under it stays `fresh`: it is a new object per call.
- A label the creation passes on is another label than one the last call passes on, whatever their origin: `a = app f 1`
  then `λ⊤ → (app f 2; a)` calls `f` once at creation, and its answer is what the value holds, while the second call's
  would be new at each call.
- **A created object is never apart from `own`.** Within one activation a site is apart from any parameter: the parameter
  was there first. `own` comes later, so it may be that very object, an earlier call's answer: `λv → [ xs, v ]` called
  as `g (g [])[0]` holds `xs` twice. So in a called code the distinct check (§2.9.3) gives `no` for entries that hold
  such an object and a part of `own`, and `overlap` says `may`.

**At the caller.** A call of a value that is the result of a walked call `q` at a function slot `s`, `q`'s callee a code
`D` with `D@s` (or a contract that publishes one), and that is not one parameter's slot (rule 1 above comes first), is a
call of `built(closure, D@s, kids = q's arguments, the value)`. A label applied to such a value is a virtual call of the
same closure. Both are decided from the code's numbering and the position's slot, so they are known at the walk,
before any contract of `D`'s group is. A value that is not such a reference (a label's answer, a supply, `⊤`, the
result of a called code) stays what §2.11.3 says: unknown code, or an escape.

**Recursion and the bound.** `D@s` calls `D` in its creation and may call `D@s` in its last call: both are members of
`D`'s group, and `§2.12` solves them with `D`. `previous ⊤` in `grow`'s second lambda is a label of that lambda, on a
capture. Applied in `grow@ε`'s walk, the capture is `grow (n - 1)`'s result, so it is a virtual call of `grow@ε`, and
the answer is the least fixed point of `fresh ∪ answer`, which is `fresh`. A chain of levels (`ClosureTower`, `wk`
over two closures of `w(k-1)`) has a called contract per level, of constant size: `wk@ε` answers what the arms of its
last call answer, in `wk`'s parameters, `self` and `fresh`, so no creation context is enumerated and none is written
down. Every level's cost is its own, one more walk of a body. The tower is bounded by construction, with no limit to trip.

**Why not the code and its captures as arrivals.** An arrival naming a code with arrivals for its captures has no
finite form on `grow` (its capture is its own result, whose capture is its own result) and doubles on `ClosureTower`.
It needs a fold, and each fold needs an argument that it is sound. The called contract *is* that fold: the captures are
closed over by `D`'s parameters and `self`, so what stays is what the call does.

**A value's lambda** (*amended 2026-11-06, #2132*). A declaration with no parameters whose body is a lambda or a
constructor has a
called contract at `ε`: the one place it publishes what a call of it does (§2.11.1). It bends this section's
convention in two ways, and only here. Its slot is `ε` of the **value**, not of a function's result, since the value has
no result to stand in; and it is the lambda's or the constructor's own contract, not a called code: its parameters are the function type's
own and nothing else, with no `self` and no `D` parameters. That is exact, since `D` has none, and the body of a
declaration with no parameters has no parameter to capture, and `armContracts` takes an arm only with no captures, so
no read of the value can make its objects another's. `Callees.importedCall` reads it only at the call's arity. Nothing else meets it: `Called.value` asks `calledOf` of a walked call's contract, and
a value's own contract is never that of a call. No format change: a block already writes a contract's called
contracts (§3.6, version 23). A choice, `case` or `let` whose arms are all such codes has their join there, and any other value has none (§2.11.1).

**Which slots.** `ε` of a function result and, below it, a record's field or a tuple's part, on through records and
tuples (`{ run = λ⊤ → … }`). A slot's type has to be read to know its parameters, and a constructor's argument needs
the type's definition instantiated: a function in a `Maybe`, or under a `[*]`, a `◆` or a `⟲`, has none and is what it
was. Only a declaration's body has them: a local function's or a lambda's result is what it was. Each is a walk, so a
declaration pays once per function slot of its result, and at most `below_min` (16) slots a declaration, by field rank:
a tuple of tuples doubles its slots. `D@s` of a called code does not exist: what a call of a function value answers is
unknown code when it is called in turn. Each of these is a precision gap of the `⊤` kind, never a change of what is
checked (#2039).

**Sound.** Take any call `g a` that runs a value `v` that `D(b)` returned at `s`. It runs a code `K` with `v`'s captures
(§2.11.4). `D@s`'s last call is that run, with `own` for `a` and `D`'s parameters for `b`: every activation of `D` is one
of the paths of the walk, and the second walk reads the same body, with the same contracts, as the first. So:

1. Every object the run reaches comes from `a`, from `b`, from what `v` holds, or from the run. By the read-off's cases
   these are `own`'s, `D`'s and `self`'s arrivals and `fresh`, and §2.11.2 instantiates each on the call's arguments. A
   leaf the walk cannot name is `⊤` (O1).
2. Every write the run makes of `a` or `b` is a write of the contract, a demand at the call; one of what `v` holds is
   refused where the closure left `D`, or is a cell operation. Nothing changed in `Closures`: a closure in a result, or
   handed back, has escaped there, so a writer is refused as it was, and the `once` rules stand. A value a caller loses
   (in a cell, to unknown code) has the same escape behind it. So this is only an answer's precision.
3. Every call of `v` that reaches `g a` is a call of `D@s`, with a count of its own, so labels add up as for any call,
   and each is one activation of the code the label names, supplied by the run. Nothing is run that no label names:
   the §2.11.3 case split gains a case for a call and one for a label (a known code, by another name).
4. The creation's facts are dropped from `D@s` and read at `D`'s call instead, once. They happened before `g a`, and
   `g`, a holder of everything `D` left in the value, was live from there to the call (`k.use` of the callee, whole).
5. The answer of a call may be a capture, so a holder of the answer holds it (`alias`, `later-use`); a capture answered
   twice is one object twice; a `self` arrival is every object the value holds at the caller, which is what `res` says
   of it, deep. A copy of the answer is a new object (#2030: `c = List.copy a`, then `c` is no capture). A condition read
   off `D@s` compares objects of one run of the code: two created objects are as apart as the creation left them, a
   created object and `D`'s parameter too (it was made after it), a `fresh` of the run and anything too, and a created
   object and `own` are not called apart.
6. The group's rounds are §2.12's: a candidate `D@s` reads only what a member's draft says, the validation walk is an
   ordinary walk under the candidates, and a code outside its candidate is joined.

Refused that a perfect checker accepts: a `self` arrival is everything the value holds, so two captures of one
closure are one object to a holder (the second `ClosureTower` arm's list is not the first's, and the write is still
refused: `run/ClosureTower`), and a returned writer stays refused at the return. Fixtures:
`ownership/ReturnedClosureAnswer`, `ownership/CopyOfClosureAnswer`, `ownership/RecordFieldLambda`,
`run/SanitiserReturnedClosure` (fifteen shapes, each refused), `run/SanitiserReturnedClosureApart` (eleven, each
accepted in place), `run/SanitiserReturnedClosureImported`.

The review of #2045 found the two bullets above by the sanitiser (`creationAnswer`, `madeBesideOwn` in
`run/SanitiserReturnedClosure`), and #2048: a value of the frame that may hold a function, handed to a call, is used whole there, since the
callee may run it and no footprint says so. Otherwise a closure's holdings were not live at `List.update`, `Ref.update` or
`Ref.modify`, directly or through a helper (`run/SanitiserRowCallbackHolds`, trapping on master too). It is a use of the local,
not a read in a contract, and a frame's parameter has no such use: its caller makes that use, and a read there would be an
operand at every pass, asking a `taken` row's elements plain. That leaves a parameter's holdings not live at a row, which traps on master and here (#2050).

*As built (2026-11-05).* `Called.zig`, `Made.zig`; a walk's `Called.Last` marks where each list's last call begins, zero
for any other code, so that every reader takes `items[last..]` and no other code changes. `Groups.calledCodes` numbers
the called codes after the body, so a group's order walks them after the nested codes. A contract keeps its called
contracts in `Contract.Table.called`, a run a contract, and a block writes them after the contract, in the canonical order
of their slots (§3.6, version 23). A called code's label carries `Called.last_origin`, since no instruction has its type.
`summary f@.get` is its dump line; it has no `account` line, and its records are charged to `f`'s. Measured (Debug, one
job, against master at `db3480e28`): 1 018 oracle probes: 0 DIFF, 1 TRAP, on master too, of a label's answer (#2036), two
more accepted; a generated sweep of 1 820 programs (26 ways to make a closure × 10 ways to call it × 7 things to do with
the answer): 0 TRAP, 0 DIFF, 710 master refused accepted, none master accepts refused. The review sweeps' 11 312
programs: 0 TRAP, 0 DIFF. The ledger of 2 361 roots, by position, against master at `fae30693b`: 32 refused → accepted (15 of them the new
fixtures), and 3 accepted → refused, all `run/SanitiserRowCallbackHolds`, whose programs trap on master (#2048). Cost: core's
3.3 s unchanged, every root's records +0.6 %, growth unchanged everywhere, the highest declaration ×2.9
(`Tea.startAfter`, one body walked twice), and `ClosureTower` flat at 939 records a level at depths 1, 8, 16 and 24 (503
before), growth 0.

#### 2.11.4 Closures

A `lambda` (also `f a _`, which `Lower` makes a lambda) and a local function (`let_def` with parameters) are
codes of their own. Their parameters are their own, then their **captures**: the enclosing frames' locals
the body reads, in local order. The body is walked as its own frame, and its contract is read off as any
code's. A block's local functions that call each other are a group, solved as §2.12 solves a declaration
group.

*Amended 2026-11-03 (#1745): a parameter written as a pattern.* A code's parameter place is its local's type for a
name (`λx`) and, for a pattern (`λ( k, v )`, `λ⊤`), the parameter's place in the code's own function type: the
lambda's, or the local function's. Before, it was the pattern instruction's type, which the checker does not
record, so the place was a type variable's and what the pattern bound was lost: `Dict.fromList`'s result said
only `shared`, `List.map xs λ( _, v ) → v` said its elements were fresh, and an edit in place of a list the
result held ran under it (`run/SanitiserLambdaPattern`; the sanitised runs trapped). With the bindings kept, a
callback's write of a pattern's part is a write of its supply, which a worded row with a callback reads as
unknown code (`List.update`'s `focus`): those writes are refused at the call until the row is read (#1704).

*Amended 2026-11-03 (#1752): a `taken` callback's row is read.* `focus : written returned List a, borrowed Int,
once taken stored (a → a) → List a` gives its callback a label: called `once` (`many` without the word), its one
supply `π1[*]` slot for slot, kept by nothing, and with `stored` its answer arrives at the result's `[*]`. The
rest of the list stays, so what the callback writes must occur nowhere else in it (§2.13.6, *the container is
exclusive*): each write of the supply at slot `s` relies, at the caller, on `π1{[*]*~, [*]·s}` — the written
objects once, apart from everything else the elements hold. The label's origin carries a mark (bit 30 of its
offset) that a pass keeps, so the condition is asked wherever the callback is known, also through a helper that
passes it on; a supply that is no parameter's slot there was judged at the pass. Measured on `List.update xs 0
λv → List.push v 2`: accepted for fresh elements and for rows that share only keys the callback does not
write; refused for `[ a, a ]`, through a helper, and for a list at another path of another element. Asked of
nothing, or with the mark lost at a pass, the sanitised runs of `run/SanitiserListUpdateShared` show the stale
read; asked `[*]*` plain, rows that share a key the callback does not write are refused.
*Amended 2026-11-03 (#1760):* the mark is kept by a label a known code passes on **inside** the taken callback, as
well as by the callback itself: `upd rs f = List.update rs 0 λv → f v` hands `f` the element through a lambda
that the row's label runs. There the label of `f` that `upd` passes on had the lambda's call `f v` as its
origin, without the mark, so its supply `π1[*]` was asked nothing at `upd`'s callers, and `upd [ k, k ] λv →
List.push v 5` edited `k` in place while the other element held it (`run/SanitiserListUpdateForward`; the
sanitised run trapped). Now a label passed on from a virtual call that a `taken` label runs, at any level
outward, carries the mark in its origin. Sound because what such a label is supplied is what the `taken` label
supplied, or a part of it, or objects that are not the row's at all. The condition is then asked of its param
arrivals. An arrival from elsewhere only asks more. Fresh elements, and rows that share only a key the callback
does not write, are still accepted (`run/SanitiserListUpdateForwardApart`).
*Amended 2026-11-05 (#1954 review): the condition of a supply passed on by structure.* The condition was read
off the supply's root: its first parameter arrival `a` gave `π{a*~, a·s}` for a write at `s`. A label passed on
projects its supply by structure (§2.11.3), so for an element that holds no object of its own (a tuple, a
constructor, a `Maybe`) the root lists the parts, `ε π1[*].0 π1[*].1, .0 π1[*].0, .1 π1[*].1`, or nothing at all
(inside a forwarding lambda). The write of `.1` then asked `π1{[*].0*~, [*].0·.1}`, a slot below the wrong part,
or nothing, and `upd rs f = List.update rs 1 f` with `upd [ ( a, v ), ( b, v ) ] λ( k, vs ) → ( k, List.push vs 8 )`
pushed onto `v` in place while the other row held it. So did a key write, a forwarding lambda, two helpers, a
helper that updates twice, nested tuples, three-tuples, constructors, `Maybe` and a lambda that swaps the parts
(`run/SanitiserPassedTupleRow`; the sanitised runs trapped). Now a write at `s` asks, at the caller, every
parameter arrival of the supply deep and apart, and plain the arrivals of the deepest entry at a prefix `p` of
`s` (and of an open entry at a prefix), each continued by the rest of `s`. Sound because the supply's arrivals
name every caller slot whose objects the callback is handed, so together they are the element whose objects
must be apart from the written ones, as `π1[*]*~` was; and the entry at the longest prefix, or an open one,
names where the written slot's objects come from, as the root did when it held the element: a shorter entry
that is not open names a part, whose steps do not continue to `s`. Where the element has an object of its
own, the root and the entries say the same as before. Rows that share only a key the callback does not write,
fresh rows, and parts swapped onto apart rows are still accepted (`run/SanitiserPassedTupleRowApart`).

The value of a lambda is `built(closure, site ι, kids = the captures' values at creation)`: the closure holds
its captures, so a holder of the closure holds them (§2.8 *Dead*: `captured`). Calling a closure value is a
call of its code with the arguments and the captured values. A function declaration used as a value is a
closure with no capture; a constructor used as a value is the constructor's code. A field capture `(x, .f)`
is a read at creation (R-5.4.6), a whole capture is used wherever the closure is consumed (R-5.4.1). A body
that writes a capture makes its code `once` (R-2.8): its creation is a `once` demand on each written capture,
and a second call of the closure, a call by a label whose `calls` is many, or an escape of the closure
refuses it. A code that writes one of its own **parameters** relies on its callers' supplies; where the closure
escapes (to a callee with the pessimistic contract, to JavaScript, into a cell), its callers are unknown, so each
such write is a `callsite` demand on `⊤` at the first escape, refused `unknown` (O1; `Closures.zig`). A `once`
code's capture write at its escape, at its capture by another closure (which may call it any number of times), or at a label of a callee that may call it again (`calls` many, or two labels
of one function slot), is refused `once`.

*Amended 2026-11-02 (#1727):* a **cell operation** on a captured `Ref` is not a write of a capture for `once`. A
cell operation is a shallow write of a `◆` slot (`Ref.set`, `Ref.update`, `Ref.modify`: the `cellwrite` rows of
§2.13.7, `Eval.cellWrite`). It rewrites the cell, which is the shared mutable place, so a second call stales no
reader. A closure whose only capture writes are cell operations is therefore not `once`: a callee that calls it many
times (`Task.retry`, `Task.forever`, `Browser.Events.eachAnimationFrameDelta`, a recursive walker), its escape and
its capture by another closure refuse nothing. Its creation is a `writer` demand on each written cell's `◆`
instead, `cell r◆` in the dump, so the enclosing code's contract still says `writes π◆`: a projection of a
captured record (`m.world◆`) names the `◆` of each cell slot it reaches, never the handle. Before this, such a
closure was `once`, and the callees above refused it. An **in-place write of a captured list** still makes the code
`once`, under the rules above, also beside cell operations in the same body. A list taken out of the cell under
`cellupdate`/`cellmodify` and edited in place is a write of that row's callback parameter: at that callback it is
judged by the row's own rules (§2.13.7). *Amended 2026-11-02 (#1729):* for the closure around the operation, the
edit is a write of the captured cell's contents (deep at its `◆`, `writes π◆*`), not a cell operation, so it makes
the closure `once` as a captured list's write does. A run of the closure may leave a loan of the contents live
when the next run edits them: the `Ref.get r` it answers to `List.map`, or a loan that another fiber holds across
a suspension, which v2 does not check yet. Before #1729 the edit was refused at the callback (`unknown`), so the
closure's contract did not have it. *Amended 2026-11-02 (#1734):* this `once` is one of the two rules that keep
v2 sound across fibers when it has no suspension rule (§2.13.7, *loans across a suspension*). A closure that a fiber
starter (`Task.par`, `race`, `spawn`, …) is given is escaped, so its edit in place is refused there. If the edit is
exempt from `once`, `run/SanitiserFiberBranch` reads a list that another branch changed while it slept.

A function value returned by a callee is unknown code at the caller (§2.11.3): its answer is `⊤`. *Amended 2026-11-05
(#2028):* unless a called contract follows it (§2.11.3, *a function value in a result*). *Amended
2026-11-02 (#1709):* so a closure that a callee **hands back** — an arrival of the callee's `res` (itself,
`same f = f`; captured by a closure the callee returns, `later f = λx → f x`; in a record, `{ run = f }`) — has
escaped at that call: the caller's later call of it is unknown code that instantiates none of its writes, so
its parameter writes are `callsite` demands on `⊤` there, refused `unknown`, and a capture write is refused
`once`, as at any escape. Before this, the hand-back was not an escape, and the write the code accepted as
`param` ran on a list the caller still read (`same λl → List.push l 1` applied to `xs`, then `xs` read).
*Amended 2026-11-03 (#1773):* a parameter's function slot a callee hands back is followed when the value is that
slot by every arrival, and escapes otherwise; a known code's answer to a label escapes the parameters' function
slots it holds as well as its closures (§2.11.3, *a function value goes where a value goes*).

*Amended 2026-11-03 (#1758): a captured closure called by a closure.* `g = λv → List.push v 5`, `h = λv → g v`,
`h k`: `h`'s call of its capture `g` is a label of `h`, and at `h k` the label is applied to `g`'s code (§2.11.3).
Two rules were missing. (1) **The site's type.** A label's supplies are read at the call site's function type,
never the code's own (a let-bound `g` is `List number → List number`, a type variable's place). A capture has no
argument instruction at the call, so the site's type is the type the label's origin call has its callee at (the
head of `g v` in `h`, `List Int → List Int`). Where neither is to hand, the code is read as unknown, and then it
**escapes at that call**: it still runs, so its parameter writes are `callsite` demands on `⊤`, refused
`unknown`, and a capture write is `once`, as at any escape. Before, the unknown read dropped the code's writes,
and `h k` made no demand. (2) **Every label outward.** Where the call a label is applied at is itself a virtual
call (`apply2 k k λv → g v`: the lambda's label of `g`, applied inside `apply2`'s label), the written supply is
the outer virtual call's parameter, so it is that outer label's supply in turn: an arrival of it at the supply's
entry carries the write's slot outward. The write relies on each such label's supply condition and, for a
`taken` row, its container occurrences, at that label's call, and a slot any of them keeps refuses. Before, only
the innermost label's condition was asked, and `apply2 k k`, `List.map [ m, m ]` and `List.update [ k, k ] 0`
through `λv → g v` were accepted. Sound because the chain follows the supply through every label it is handed
by, each step an arrival (§2.10), so each object the write reaches is judged by every callee that handed it;
the chain ends, as a virtual call always follows the call it applies a label of. Fixtures
`run/SanitiserCapturedWriter` (refused; the sanitised runs trapped) and `run/SanitiserCapturedWriterApart` (the
same shapes on apart or fresh lists, accepted in place).

**A virtual call is an evaluation's** (#2166). A contract's labels are sorted by `(j, slot, origin)`, so a label's index
moves when the contract gains a label before it, and a candidate gains labels from round to round. An index means
something only in the contract it was read from. So **nothing that outlives an evaluation holds an index in a contract.**
What holds one is the evaluation's and goes with it: `known`, `label_map`, `lent`, `applied` and `passes`, and every
`cb(i)` read, each against the contract the evaluation read at that call.

A virtual call follows from what an evaluation reads: the labels of the contract read at a call, and the value at each
label's slot. So each evaluation makes its virtual calls and their supplies from nothing (`Eval.evaluate`, `Virtual.zig`):
`Frame.calls` is cut back to the walk's, and `Frame.supplies` is emptied. No table of them lasts between rounds, a
virtual call of a label that has gone cannot be read, and a code read as unknown escapes in every evaluation. A key of a
supply is its index in `Frame.supplies`, which is the evaluation's too.

The roots these calls make stay in the frame, as the values `valueAt` makes do. A root from an earlier evaluation is
unreachable: only a virtual call's arguments and its answer lead to one, and they are made again. A leaf `fresh` of a
virtual call's index is read through `Frame.calls` as it stands. The kept judgements of §2.12 compare ids only when the
group's print says the round read what the one before it read, and then the evaluation is the same one, with the same
numbers. The cost is charged: one root and its leaves per virtual call per round. Measured: core's records +0.12 %
(2 097 776 → 2 100 314), a tower of 64 labelled closures +3.8 %, 26 rounds of labels through a group +0.3 %.

`Frame.cbs` does last, since a derived label's record is a name a leaf `answer` holds. So what asks which labels run reads
this evaluation's: `AnswerKeep.repeats` counts a direct label or one passed on now. It answers *yes* to let a holder off
(`AnswerKeep.kept`, `Supplied`), so a label only an earlier evaluation met must not add to it.

Before, a virtual call was kept under `(q, li)`. In `List.foldl … λi acc → ( k0 acc.2, List.foldl … λj s → k1 s, k2
acc.0 )` the lambda gains `k1`'s label a round after `k2`'s and `k0`'s and sorts it first. Index 0 went from `k2`'s label to
`k1`'s, index 1 from `k0`'s to `k2`'s, and the records stayed: `k2`'s label applied `k0`'s code, so what `k2` answers
never held its capture `q`. The program was accepted and trapped, and a `let` moved gave a refusal. A code read as
unknown made its escape once, in the evaluation that made the record, so the next evaluation's verdict went without it. Fixtures
`run/SanitiserLabelRounds`, `run/SanitiserLabelRoundsOrder` (refused) and `run/SanitiserLabelRoundsApart`,
`run/SanitiserLabelRoundsCopied` (accepted; the second was refused by the wrong label's answer), `run/SanitiserWildCodeRounds` (refused, the escape) and `run/SanitiserWildCodeRoundsApart` (accepted);
`ordering_test.zig` compares the two let orders.

Measured, against master at `add0059ab`. `review-2161/g5`: 136 TRAP and 552 of 1 110 classes split by let order on master with
#2146's relation, 0 and 0 now, 2 022 programs accepted before and 2 448 now. The 120 of those g5 programs accepted before
and refused now each trap on master with #2146's relation, on shorter folds. Two generators in `s2166/` (26 760 programs:
captures through inner lambdas, nested folds, recursion through a group, record-held codes, every let and declaration
order): 0 TRAP, 0 classes split. Their 72 TRAP of the record-held family were the escape. `repeats_stale_labels`
survives: no probe reaches a stale label there. The 240 `review-2173/g9` programs it differs on hold quiet labels, which `repeats` doesn't count, and they move no verdict.

#### 2.11.5 Other constructs

- **Record update** `{ r | F = … }` builds a record: a `built` record with a fresh site, whose untouched fields
  are `r`'s projections (each a `field` use of `r`) and whose `F` fields are the new values. No storage of `r`
  is written: an in-place record update is a later slice's `update` demand (R-4.8), and until then the
  emitter copies.
- **`try`** (`e?`): the value is `e`'s success payload; the failure payload, built into the enclosing
  definition's failure constructor, is a returned alternative of that definition.
- **`markup`**: a `built` opaque value with a fresh site whose kids are every embedded value; each embedded
  value is used whole.
- **`type_dispatch`**: `⊤`, every operand used and escaped (as a wordless `foreign`, O1).
- **Schema members and constructors** (§2.13.10): the pessimistic contract. *Amended 2026-11-02 (#1685):* a
  member answers what its `via` conversions answer, which may be a top-level list, and a tagged constructor
  holds its arguments, so the former row (every argument read, the result `fresh`) let `List.push` write a
  top-level list through `apply Fixed.parse input` (SchemaMemberHanded).
- **A `method_call`**: the code `Dispatch` names, as a `call`; unresolved, the pessimistic contract.
  *Amended 2026-11-05 (#2029):* `r.f x` on a record field of function type is a call of the field's value, as `f = r.f; f x`
  is: a lambda built in the frame is a code call, a parameter's field a label, any other value what §2.11.3 says.
  Before, the dispatch site's `field` term read as a method without a code, the pessimistic contract, so the
  lambda was unknown, and so was a parameter's own `r.on`, whatever its callers handed. A record update replaces the
  field's value in the record the walk built, so the call reads the new field.
- **Evidence.** *Amended 2026-11-02 (#1708):* a declaration a dispatch site passes as `where`-clause evidence (every
  `top`/`ext` term of the site, however deep) is a function value of that declaration's code, made at the site and
  escaped there (§2.11.4): the binder calls it through a type variable (`x.bump 1`), an unresolved `method_call`
  that the checker cannot follow, so a parameter the declaration writes is a `callsite` demand on `⊤` at the site,
  refused `unknown`. A worded declaration is not taken: its words write only at a call site the checker
  authorises, never through a function value. Before this, the evidence site made no demand and `bump`'s `param`
  push ran on a box the caller read again (`one s`, then `s.items`).

### 2.12 Fixpoints and the pre-pass

*Replaced 2026-11-02 (#1685), with §2.3, §2.9–§2.11; the pre-pass paragraph at the end is unchanged.*

A non-recursive code is walked once: its callees' contracts are known, and its contract is read off its walk.

**A recursive group** (R-5.6.1), or a block's local functions that call each other, is solved in three steps.

1. **The inference walk.** Each member is walked once, with every call of a group member left **symbolic**: the
   call's result is its call root (§2.3.2), whose expansion reads the callee's *current* candidate. Each
   candidate starts at ⊥: `returns = false`, nothing arrives, `res_cond yes`. The walk records, besides its
   values, the **edges** of the group: per group call, which caller slots its result reaches (the result
   description passing through the call's root), which of its targets and conditions read the callee's
   contract.
2. **Deliveries.** The candidates grow by delivering facts along the edges, never by walking a body again. A
   fact is an arrival at a callee's result slot, a write, a read, an escape, a label or a supply, or the
   `returns` bit. A new fact of member `g` at slot `r` is delivered along each edge `(call k of g, r → q)` of
   each caller: it is projected onto call `k`'s arguments (§2.11.2), and each projected leaf is a new fact of
   the caller (a parameter's slot is an arrival; another group call's leaf is a further delivery). Each fact is
   delivered once per edge. `res_cond` and a supply's condition only weaken and `req` only strengthens, each at
   most once per occurrence of the finite vocabulary, so the checks that read a callee's condition run again
   when it changes, and only those. `InitializationLimit.rotate`, whose answer gains one arrival per round,
   costs one delivery per arrival: linear in its parameters.
3. **The validation walk.** Each member is walked again, once, with the candidates as its group callees'
   contracts, and its contract is read off. The walk's contract must be `within` the candidate (§2.10). This
   walk's demands are the declaration's verdict lines. When a member's walk is not within its candidate, the
   candidate is joined with it and the group is validated again; this is an inference defect, counted on the
   account line (`walks`), and the corpus requires two walks per member.

An empty recursive result is ⊥ until a returning alternative gives it a value: a `case` arm whose value is
`bot` is dropped, a construction or call with a `bot` operand is `bot`. ⊥ applies to the result only; reads,
writes and escapes executed before a recursive call are the walk's, whatever the call returns.

**As built** [#1685]. Step 2 runs every member's evaluation open at once (`Deliver.zig`). A call of a
member reads the member's growing draft: its instantiation (§2.11.2) is a **key**, `(call, caller slot)`, whose
leaves only grow, and each consumer of a key (a description of the result, a parameter effect, a supply, an
escape, another key) **subscribes** to it and gets every leaf once, the ones there when it subscribed and each
one added later. A member's new arrival is delivered to the keys that read its slot (an open slot's to every
key below it), a new write or escape to the calls of it. Conditions (`res_cond`, `req`, a supply's) and
labels are read from the candidates of the round before, so a round is the facts delivered to a fixed point
plus one evaluation of the conditions; rounds repeat while a candidate read moved. The validation round
(step 3) evaluates each code plainly under the candidates; a code within its candidate publishes the contract
that round read off (no reliance an earlier round made and a later one dropped), one outside it is joined,
counted as `inference defects` on the account line, and validated again. A group in which no evaluation read
another member's draft was a plain evaluation already and is not validated again. Measured (Debug, one job):
`rotate` with 2, 4, 8, 15, 30 and 60 lists costs 451, 647, 1 050, 1 761, 3 294 and 6 324 records in three
rounds; generic `removeMin` 23 633, core's `Dict.removeMin` 23 715, `Dict.descend` 30 659, all with growth 0.
A call's whole subtree of more than 16 slots is read through **one key below its position**
(`Relation.instBelow`): the callee's entries at and below it, each at its own caller slot, and its open
entries above it. An atom, or a call's result, that an open entry gives holds once for the subtree below its
slot; any other open arrival is its projection at the slot, read once, and each slot below through that
slot's own key; a plain entry's atom is itself at its slot. Measured after it (2026-11-02): generic
`removeMin` 23 539, `Dict.removeMin` 23 621, `Dict.descend` 24 422, `Schema.madeNode` 21 625,
`Schema.shapeOf` 290 571 (its source continuation is 310 272) and `Schema.shapesOf` 20 418, all with growth 0.

*Specified 2026-11-03 (#1714): judgements kept across rounds.* Each round evaluates every code from nothing
and judges every demand again. In `rot a₁ … aₙ k` (`GroupRotate`), which calls itself with its lists
rotated by one, the callee's candidate gains one parameter's write a round, so there are n + 2 rounds and
each judges n demands against n operands: growth 58 290 of 65 536 at n = 64, `Resolve.resolve` 97 % of it.
A verdict from round r is stale in round r + 1 only where something it read moved. So:

- **A judgement records what it read** of the candidates: for each group callee and each field it read
  (`res`, `reads`, `writes`, `escapes`, `req`, a label), that field's tree node for the one parameter it read
  (or the result's node), by dense id, as the candidate stood. The reads it makes through the frame (a later
  use's footprint, an operand's projection, an escape) name the call whose callee they read, so they record
  the same. The relies of a call (`C.req` instantiated, item 4) are the call's, made once a round, and a
  demand records only that it relied on them.
- **A demand is the same demand in the next round** when its key is: the walk's demand sites are fixed by
  the walk; a call's write demand is `(call, parameter, write node)`. The keys index flat arrays by dense id,
  the round's state beside the walk's.
- **Re-judging.** In round r + 1, a demand whose recorded nodes are all the candidates' nodes now keeps its
  judgement, its verdict and the occurrences it gathered (§2.9.4); any other is judged again. Contract trees
  are hash-consed (§2.10), so "the same node" is one comparison of ids, and it is exact: an unchanged node is
  an unchanged fact. The validation round (step 3) judges every demand of every code, as before, and its
  verdicts are the lines.
- This is the fixpoint's own state across its rounds, as the distinct check's rounds keep theirs (§2.9.3):
  never a table of earlier answers to unrelated questions. `rot` re-judges the demands of the parameters
  whose nodes moved: one a round.

**As built** [#1714] (`Kept.zig`). A demand's key is its fields (point, kind, base, call, argument,
pending clock, `relies.no`, the `kept`/`many`/`callback` bits) with its targets' leaves and its
operands' values; leaves are interned, so equal lists are equal objects. A judgement records the later
uses' footprints it read, each `(call, parameter)` with the callee's read and write tree node of that
parameter (`Later.Uses.feet`, `Descent.cover`), and where it stood in the round's **holder events**: a
holder keyed, a hold done, a holder's aggregated holds done (§2.8's sweep), the state that later
judgements read. It is taken again only when the round's events so far are the round before's, event for
event; it then makes its own events again (a keying by keying the live holders, as it did) and its
operand and pending writes, for `req`. What no key names is compared once a round, whole: each member's
candidate (result node, result condition, labels with their supplies, flags), its draft's result and
labels as the expansions read them live, and each frame's escapes. This is coarser than the spec's node
per field read for the result (a moved result re-judges the round), and exact. Only demands are kept; a
label's supplied parts are judged every round. Under `-Downership-full-cross-check` every demand is
judged and a kept judgement it would have taken is compared with it (line, events, writes); a difference
panics. Measured (Debug, one job): `rot` with 8, 16, 32 and 64 lists costs 6 799, 21 712, 76 799 and
287 898 records (8 377, 28 522, 105 321 and 406 404 before), growth 0 of 65 536 at 64 (51 561 before);
its demand records fall from 198 658 to 58 232. The cost table's other rows are unchanged.

**Termination.** The vocabulary is finite: the slots are fixed by the types, the arrivals by the parameters'
slots and the labels by the instructions. Every delivered fact is added once; every condition moves at most
once per occurrence. The account (§4.4) bounds the work in records, reserved before work. *As built:* a group
past 4 096 rounds fails `ownership_limit` (`Groups.zig`). It is loud, and it accepts nothing.

**Soundness.** The validation walk is an ordinary walk under the candidates. A post-fixed point of the
contract transfer is a sound summary of every activation of the group by induction on the activation tree,
since a candidate that the walk stays within describes each recursive call's result at least as widely as the
body can produce it. The deliveries only compute that candidate faster; nothing they compute is trusted
without the validation walk.

**The BIR pre-pass** (`Prepass.zig`, L3, reads the BIR, the dispatch table and the graph): SCC edges come
from `check/Edges.declEdges`, including ordinary refs, every resolved dispatch/evidence call site and
derived bodies; no locally reconstructed two-tag approximation; alias chains of function values (R-5.5.6); read counts of private parameterless values (R-4.9.3);
the enclosing frame of each lambda (for the dynamic summary-dependency edges of §2.10);
the spread chains `Lower` recorded (§2.13.2). `Groups` supplies semantic targets for a type's `eq`/`compare`
and `withDefault (map m f) d` recognition (§2.13.12). Resolve those through the lowerer's well-known symbols
at the adapter boundary; Prepass itself neither compares declaration-name strings nor owns class resolution.

### 2.13 Reductions: every surface construct to the core

1. **Constructors as values** (R-4.8.10, R-5.5.8, R-5.5.12): a constructor's class from its type: `res` a `node` at
   the type's place with `C#i ↦ πᵢ`, every πᵢ `A`; a record-alias constructor is a record literal. `Pushed : Value →
   Msg` holds a crossing value: `res ∅`. Constructors are rebuilt, never written (R-4.8.9).
2. **Lists** (R-2.2, R-2.3, R-2.13, R-4.4): `Lower.lowerSpreadList` (`Lower.zig:2563-2611`) lowers a spread literal
   to right-nested `List.cons`/`List.append` calls stamped with the `…` token. **A BIR fact replaces reading those
   calls back**: `Lower` also records, per declaration, each spread chain as `Bir.Spread{ root call, items (inst,
   is_spread) in source order }` in `extra` (`Decl.spreads_start/end`), with no change to the instructions the type
   checker and the emitter read. `Transfer` evaluates the chain as one instruction at its root: `[ x₁…xₖ, …xs ]`
   (one spread, last) is a **prepend**: cells `{site ι}` ∪ `cellsAt(xs, ε)` approximate (re-cons may answer the
   base, R-4.4.2), `[*] ↦ join(x₁…xₖ, proj(xs, [*]))`, a positional collection whose κ is the construction
   rule's, as the `prepended` row's (`excl` of each front, `excl xs[*]`, `apart` of the fronts and `xs[*]`; #1386:
   it was `lost`, which refused every `[ x, …xs ]` handed to a callee owing `excl π1[*]`); the storage's κ `lost`
   — **except** when every front item is a `List` whose
   `ε` cells are a non-empty set of `site`/`result` cells not escaped and not in `reach(xs)`, or whose *instruction*
   is a record literal, a constructor application or a tuple (fresh objects by construction, whatever their cells —
   a tuple's and constructor's cells are `∅`): then `{site ι}` alone (R-4.4.3, `p/PrependFreshRecord`); a scalar, parameter,
   capture, taken element, top-level value or callback result keeps the base's cells (`call (a)`). Anything after
   the first spread is a `construction` demand with base = the first spread's operand, each stored item lowering κ,
   a spread literal inside another's last spread its own write. `[ …xs ]` is `xs` and records no spread fact (including nested single spreads);
   every recorded root is a distinct call made by that literal. A literal is a fresh `site`
   (R-4.10.5); `++` chains per R-2.2. The emitted prepend writes no existing array (R-4.4.4): the lowering's
   obligation, asserted under runtime safety.
3. **Patterns and views** (R-2.14, R-4.5): `[ x, …rest ]` on `n`: `x ↦ elem(c·ι)` per container cell
   `c ∈ cellsAt(n, ε)` (§2.2: the position of `c`'s `[*]` taken at ι),
   `rest ↦` a node with `n`'s `ε` cells (a view shares the storage) and `[*] ↦ others(c·ι)`; the split records
   the container's interpretation at ι: its κ snapshot projected through `[*]`, κ(n, `[*]`·q) at each path q (§2.9).
   **A match on a rest splits the rest's own positions** (#1390). A rest of split ι is a view of `c`'s storage, so
   its `ε` cells are `c`'s, and a second list pattern ι′ on it used to split `c` again: `elem(c·ι′)` against the
   first match's `elem(c·ι)` is two splits of one container, `under_kappa`, which a `sep` or a reliance reads as
   `lost`. Instead, where the matched value's `[*]` holds `o = others(c·ι)` for a container cell `c` of its `ε`
   (`o` may itself be a split of positions, the rest of a rest), ι′ splits `o`: `x ↦ elem(o·ι′)` and
   `rest′ ↦ [*] ↦ others(o·ι′)`. A split of `o` is a split of positions, not of a list: it is made at `o`'s own
   place and adds no step, so its refinements' canonical position is `c[*]`, as `o`'s is. Its κ is the rest's at
   `[*]`, which is ι's. The positions of the two matches are then two sides of ι (`elem(c·ι)` against a
   refinement of `others(c·ι)`, under κ(ι)), and two positions of the inner match are two sides of ι′, so
   `[ a, …rest ] → case rest of [ c ] → …` compares `a` and `c` exactly. The inner positions are refinements of
   the rest's positions, not index offsets into `c`: positions are numbered per item of one pattern (`[ a, …r, z ]`
   numbers `z` 1, from the end), so an offset would need the list's length, which no cell knows. Two different
   matches of one rest stay two splits of `o`, `under_kappa`, because they may take one position. A `c` is
   split as well, as before, when the value's `[*]` holds anything else at `c[*]`'s canonical position: `c[*]`
   itself (a join of the rest with the whole list), or a position stored beside the rest by a join with `[ a ]`, a
   push, `List.set`, `++` or the literal `[ a, …rest ]`. No split of `o` stands for that `a`, so dropping it made
   `c` look apart from `a` (#1390's review; `PatternPositionsStored`). The chain is as deep as the nesting of the matches. A constructor pattern on a recursive place materialises `level(c·ι)` for the matched node's
   non-recursive arguments and one `below(c·C#i·ι)` per recursive child step, pairwise apart under κ (R-4.7.1,
   R-4.7.7: `l`'s lists and `r` are two `below`s; `p/WriteOneLevel`); a pattern nested two constructors deep splits
   the inner `below` again, so `v` and `v2` of `Node (Node l v r) v2 r2` are distinct cells; a non-recursive
   constructor's arguments are plain projections. `List.tail`/`List.drop` are views because their bodies call the
   `view` primitive, whose words say `returned` at `ε` (R-4.5.1). Rebuilding the matched shape is a prepend over
   the view (R-2.14).
   **A list pattern reads its list** [M 2026-11-01, #1530]. A list pattern tests the length of the list it
   matches (`[]`, `[ x, …_ ]`, `[ a, b ]`, `[ …_, z ]`), so the match reads that list at the case's point,
   whatever its depth below the scrutinee. The scrutinee's `whole` use (§2.7) is the frame's read of it and
   of everything below it, so a hold in this frame needs nothing more. But read-off (§2.10) takes `R` from
   uses at their own paths, and the scrutinee's use is at its root: `skip2c r = case r of Rose [ Rose [ x,
   …_ ], …_ ] → 7` was `π1 R` alone. A caller that wrote the inner `[]` in place before calling `skip2c` on a
   value that still holds it was accepted, and the answer changed from 0 to 7; v1 refuses it. So a list
   pattern reads the parameter parts of the value it matches, as a consumed value's are read
   (`Transfer.Frame.readsOf`), and read-off marks `R` at each: `skip2c` is `π1 R, π1#Rose.0 R,
   π1#Rose.0[*]#Rose.0 R`. A refined cell reads at its canonical path, so a match below a recursive child
   reads at `⟲`, and a recursive or mutual reader's `R` closes through its group's fixpoint as any other
   mark does. `[ …rest ]` alone tests nothing and reads nothing. A constructor pattern's tag test and a
   literal pattern record no read of their own: a constructor is rebuilt, never written (item 1), the list
   that holds an element is read by the list pattern that reached the element, and a record pattern binds
   locals, whose uses are their own. Fixtures: `ownership/PatternReadsList`,
   `ownership/PatternReadsListImported`.
4. **Program entry** (R-2.10, R-5.8): a declaration with `entry` on a record parameter gives its constructor an
   entry class; at a call whose record's functions have classes: protocol by the callbacks' types (hosted with
   `settle`); `M₀ = res(init)[flags, Host := crossing]`, a top-level value `init` returns stays `shared`
   (R-5.8.3); captures of `init` move into `M₀` only when no other callback keeps them. The sparse fixpoint of
   §2.12 over `M` and κ(M) (the exclusivity invariant, R-5.8.7) with the message `msg` (symbolic, so `Got a b`'s
   payloads are `msg·#Got.0` and `msg·#Got.1`) plus the view's event-slot cells (R-5.8.9), `settle` a second
   writer (R-5.8.11). Then: `update`'s `E` on π₂, its command half, `init`'s commands, `subscriptions`' result and
   what `view`/`subscriptions` escape join Esc (R-5.8.5); each `W{F}` of `update` on `π₂·q` is an `entry` demand on
   `M@q` (Known, Unescaped, Disjoint against `msg` and the model's other paths — alternatives of one `ctor` place
   excluded, so `p/RecordVariantMove` is accepted — Dead trivially by P1; `xreq` on `(msg, M)`); a `W` on the
   message is `payload`/`entry` (R-5.8.8); a `W` of `view`/`subscriptions` on the model `read-only` (R-5.8.6). An
   unsupported shape leaves the writers pending (R-5.8.1). P1–P4, P7 and P-sync (§2.13.7) are trusted (R-5.8.13).
   browser-inline's generated root closures are no holders by the lowering interface's slot kinds (R-5.8.12).
   A platform's `entryKinds` row is a second source of an entry protocol, without the `entry` word: the worker
   `handlers` and `machine` rows of §2.13.17, which reuse this item's model fixpoint for `machine` (2026-11-02).
   *As built before S7 (2026-11-05, #1949).* The shape test is v1's, read from the worded declaration's own
   annotation (`Prepass.entryProtocol`): parameter k's type is a record written out with an `update` of two
   parameters, or of three beside a `settle` of two, where `update` answers its third parameter's type. A
   parameter worded `entry` that fails it carries no word (§2.13.6: escaped), so its callbacks are unknown code's
   and a write they make on what the runtime hands them is refused at the call, R-5.8.1's pending. Before this a
   v2 row read `entry` as a borrowed record: `settle = λstate → List.push state 0` was accepted `param` with no
   caller to check, and a runtime that read the old state after `settle` printed the written one
   (`run/SanitiserEntryUnsupported`; its twin `run/SanitiserEntrySupported` keeps the protocol and its write).
5. **Sends** (R-2.9, R-5.9): `Send msg` becomes a **nominal type** of the `browser` base platform, `pub foreign type
   Send msg`, with one operation `pub foreign pure to : Send msg, consumed msg → ⊤` (called `send.to m` by dot-call,
   or `Send.to send m`); the runtime hands a `Send` value whose sibling export is the dispatch. A send is then a
   call of a worded operation: `S` on its argument, a `send` demand on every cell of the payload (R-5.9.1), send
   values crossing (R-5.9.4); a function that sends its parameter gets `S` on it; a send handed to a callee needs the
